title: Changing and Removing Data
subtitle: UPDATE and DELETE — the two commands that can destroy a database in one keystroke.

lessons.title: UPDATE — changing what is already there
lessons.summary: SET the new value, and WHERE decides who it happens to. Forget the WHERE and you change everybody.
lessons.examTip: UPDATE table_name SET column = value WHERE condition; The WHERE clause is not optional in practice — without it every row in the table is changed.

steps.title: Data does not stand still
steps.expect: Five students. Remember Tanaka's fees — one hundred and fifty.

lines.text: Everything we have done so far has been adding and looking.
But data does not stand still. Students pay more fees. People get married and change their surname. Somebody transfers to another programme.
So we need a command that changes a record that is already sitting in the table.
That command is UPDATE, and it is powerful, and it is dangerous. I will show you both sides.
Let us see our five students first, so we know what we are starting with.
Run.
Good. Now keep your eye on Tanaka Moyo.
He has paid one hundred and fifty dollars. Remember that number. One five zero.

steps.title: Changing one record
steps.expect: Tanaka's fees change from 150 to 250. Nobody else moves.

lines.text: Tanaka has come to the office and paid another hundred dollars. So his total is now two hundred and fifty.
Watch the three lines of this command, because every UPDATE has exactly these three parts.
Line one. UPDATE students. Which table am I changing?
Line two. SET fees_paid equals two hundred and fifty. What am I changing it to?
Line three. WHERE student_id equals one. Who am I changing it for?
Which table, what change, and for whom. Three questions, three lines. Never forget the third one.
And notice I used student_id in the WHERE, not the name.
Why? Because student_id is the primary key, so I know for certain it can only be one person.
If I had said WHERE first_name equals Tanaka, and there were two Tanakas in the college, I would have changed them both.
Always target the primary key when you are changing one person. Always.
Run.
Look at Tanaka's row.
One fifty has become two fifty. His payment is recorded.
And look at everybody else. Rudo, Farai, Chipo, Blessing. Not one of them moved.
That is the WHERE doing its job. It protected the other four.

marks.cue: Line two. SET fees_paid equals two hundred and fifty
Line three. WHERE student_id equals one

steps.title: Updating a whole group, with arithmetic
steps.expect: Every NC IT student gains fifty dollars. The others are untouched.

lines.text: Now something clever, and this is a favourite exam question.
The college gives every IT student a fifty dollar bursary credit.
Now, I cannot write SET fees_paid equals fifty, because that would wipe out what they have already paid.
I want to add fifty to whatever is already there. Everybody's total is different.
So look at the SET line.
SET fees_paid equals fees_paid plus fifty.
Read that slowly. The new fees_paid equals the old fees_paid, plus fifty.
The column appears on both sides of the equals sign. That is not a mistake. That is exactly how you do arithmetic in SQL.
And the WHERE says programme equals NC IT, so it happens to a group, not to one person.
Run.
Now look down the fees column.
Tanaka went from two fifty to three hundred. Rudo from two hundred fifty to two fifty point five zero. Chipo from three twenty to three seventy.
Three students changed, all in one command, each one keeping their own starting amount.
And Farai in Accounting and Blessing in Marketing did not get the bursary, because they were not in the WHERE.
You can do the same with minus, with times, and with divide. SET price equals price times one point one five adds fifteen percent.

marks.cue: SET fees_paid equals fees_paid plus fifty
And the WHERE says programme equals NC IT

steps.title: The mistake that ends careers
steps.sql:
-- DO NOT RUN THIS ON A REAL DATABASE.
-- There is no WHERE clause, so it hits every single row.

-- UPDATE students
-- SET programme = 'NC IT';

lines.text: Now I must show you something, and I want you to feel a little bit afraid of it. That fear will protect you.
Look at the editor.
UPDATE students, SET programme equals NC IT. And then nothing. No WHERE.
I have commented it out with dashes so that it cannot run. I am not going to run this.
But understand what it would do.
With no WHERE clause, the database does not ask who. It assumes you mean everybody.
Every single student in the college would suddenly be doing NC IT. Farai in Accounting. Blessing in Marketing. All of them.
Five students here. But in a real college database, that is eight thousand records, destroyed in one keystroke.
And there is no undo. Only a backup can save you, and only if somebody made one.
So here is the habit I want you to build from today, and never break.
When you write UPDATE, type the WHERE clause first, before you type the SET.
Write the WHERE first. Then go back and fill in the SET. That way it is impossible to forget it.
Professionals do this. Now you know why.

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: The exam question sounds like this. Write an SQL statement to change the fees paid by student number one to two hundred and fifty dollars.
Your answer, three lines.
UPDATE students. SET fees_paid equals two fifty. WHERE student_id equals one. Semicolon.
And then there is a theory question that comes up again and again.
What is the effect of omitting the WHERE clause in an UPDATE statement?
Answer. All the records in the table will be updated, not just the intended ones.
One sentence, one mark, and now you will never forget it, because you have seen what it does.
Which table, what change, for whom. Three lines, every time.

lessons.title: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP
lessons.summary: Three ways to remove things, and knowing which one the question is asking for.
lessons.examTip: DELETE removes rows and can be filtered with WHERE. TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the empty table. DROP removes the table itself. This comparison is asked almost every year.

steps.title: DELETE with a WHERE
steps.expect: Farai is gone. Four students remain.

lines.text: Farai has left the college. He is not coming back, and the registrar says remove his record.
The command is short, and that is exactly what makes it dangerous.
DELETE FROM students, WHERE student_id equals three.
Notice something. There is no list of columns anywhere.
That is because DELETE always removes the entire row. You cannot delete just one field.
If you want to empty one field, that is not DELETE, that is UPDATE, setting it to NULL. Different job, different command.
Run.
Farai is gone.
Four students left. Tanaka, Rudo, Chipo, Blessing.
And notice the student numbers. One, two, four, five. There is a hole where three used to be.
That is correct behaviour, and it is important. The database will never reuse number three.
Because if it did, some old record somewhere pointing at student three would suddenly be pointing at a completely different person.
So the gap is not a bug. The gap is the database protecting your history.

marks.cue: DELETE FROM students, WHERE student_id equals three
Notice something. There is no list of columns anywhere

steps.title: Deleting a group
steps.expect: Nobody is removed this time — Farai has already gone, and nobody else owes everything.

lines.text: DELETE takes any condition, exactly like SELECT does.
Same command, different WHERE.
DELETE FROM students WHERE fees_paid equals zero.
That means, remove every student who has not paid a single cent.
Run.
Look at that. Nothing was removed.
Still four students, exactly as before.
And that is a good lesson in itself. The only student with zero was Farai, and we already deleted him.
So the condition matched nobody, and the database did nothing at all. It did not complain, and it did not break.
A DELETE that matches nothing is not an error. It is just a quiet no.

marks.cue: DELETE FROM students WHERE fees_paid equals zero

steps.title: DELETE all rows, and TRUNCATE
steps.expect: The temp_log table still exists — but it is completely empty.

lines.text: Now, what if you want to empty a whole table, but keep the table itself?
There are two ways, and the exam wants you to know the difference.
The first way is DELETE FROM table_name, with no WHERE at all. That removes every row, one by one.
The second way is TRUNCATE TABLE table_name. That empties the whole table in one action.
Watch what I build here, so we do not touch our students.
A small table called temp_log, with two entries in it. Then I truncate it. Then I look at it.
Run.
Look at the result. The table is there, but it is empty.
The columns are still standing. log_id and message. But both entries are gone.
Now the exam difference, and write this down.
DELETE is DML. It removes rows one at a time, it can have a WHERE, and it can often be rolled back.
TRUNCATE is DDL. It removes all rows at once, it cannot have a WHERE, it is faster, and it resets the auto-increment counter back to one.
DELETE picks. TRUNCATE empties. That is the shortest way to remember it.

marks.cue: The second way is TRUNCATE TABLE table_name

steps.title: DELETE versus TRUNCATE versus DROP
steps.expect: temp_log is no longer in the list of tables. students is still there.

lines.text: And now the third one, which we met in Chapter Two. DROP.
Our temp_log table is empty, but it is still standing there taking up space. Let us remove the table itself.
So watch. DROP TABLE temp_log.
And SHOW TABLES underneath, so we can see the proof.
Run.
Look at the list.
temp_log is not there any more. The table itself has stopped existing.
students is still there, safe, with our four learners inside.
Now here is the picture I want you to carry into the exam. Think of a filing cabinet drawer.
DELETE takes out the files you point at, and leaves the rest.
TRUNCATE empties the whole drawer, but the drawer is still in the cabinet.
DROP takes the drawer out of the cabinet and throws the drawer away.
Point at files. Empty the drawer. Throw the drawer away. Three commands, three pictures.

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: This comparison is asked so often that I want you to be able to write it in your sleep.
The question. Distinguish between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP.
DELETE. A DML command that removes selected records from a table, using a WHERE clause. The table structure remains.
TRUNCATE. A DDL command that removes all records from a table at once. The table structure remains, and the auto-increment counter is reset.
DROP. A DDL command that removes the entire table, including its structure and all its data.
Notice that each answer has two parts. What it removes, and what is left behind.
What it removes, and what is left behind. That is what the marker is looking for.
And one last thing before we leave this chapter, and it is the most important thing I will say all day.
Before you run any UPDATE or any DELETE on a real system, run it as a SELECT first.
Take your WHERE clause, put SELECT star FROM in front of it, and look at exactly which rows come back.
If those are the right rows, then change the word SELECT star FROM to DELETE FROM, and run it.
Test with SELECT, then destroy with DELETE. That one habit will protect you for your whole career.
